p: וַיְחִי יַעֲקֹב וְגוֹמֵר בְּמִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה לָמָּה פָּרָשָׁה זוֹ סְתוּמָה וְכוּלֵי אֶלָּא כֵּיוָן שֶׁנִּפְטַר אָבִינוּ יַעֲקֹב הִתְחִילָה שִׁעְבּוּד מִצְרַיִם דָּבָר אַחֵר מִפְּנֵי שֶׁבִּיקֵּשׁ יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ לְגַלּוֹת אֶת הַקֵּץ וְנִסְתַּם מִמֶּנּוּ דָּבָר אַחֵר מִפְּנֵי שֶׁסָּתַם מִמֶּנּוּ כָּל צָרוֹת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם.

— “Jacob lived,” and so forth. Midrash Rabbah asks why this portion is closed, and so forth: because when our father Jacob passed away, the Egyptian subjugation began. Another explanation: Jacob wished to reveal the end, but it was concealed from him. Another explanation: all the troubles of the world were closed off from him.
כָּל הַטְּעָמִים יֵשׁ לְהָבִין
— All these explanations require understanding.

אֲבָל עִיקַּר הַמְכוּוָּן עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (ריו ב) מַה כָּתוּב לְעֵילָא וַיֵּשֶׁב יִשְׂרָאֵל וְגוֹמֵר וְכָתוּב וַיְחִי יַעֲקֹב דְּלָא אִתְחֲזֵי לְאַפְרָשָׁא בֵּין דָּא לְדָא וְכוּלֵי
— Their principal meaning follows the holy Zohar (216b): what is written above? “Israel dwelt,” and so forth, followed by “Jacob lived”; no separation should appear between them, and so forth.
וְאָמַרְנוּ דְּעִיקַּר הַפְסָקוֹת הַפָּרָשִׁיּוֹת לִיתֵּן רֶיוַח לְמֹשֶׁה לְהִתְבּוֹנֵן בֵּין פָּרָשָׁה לְפָרָשָׁה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב רֵישׁ תּוֹרַת כֹּהֲנִים.
— We have explained that the main purpose of breaks between sections is to give Moses space to reflect between sections, as stated at the beginning of Torat Kohanim.
וְלָכֵן בְּכָאן אֵין שׁוּם פָּרָשָׁה שֶׁאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹם תְּפִיסָה אֵיךְ אַחַר דִּכְתִיב וַיֵּשֶׁב יִשְׂרָאֵל וְגוֹמֵר וַיֵּאָחֲזוּ בָהּ שֶׁהָיָה לָהֶם אֲחִיזָה בְּמִצְרַיִם.
— There is therefore no section break here, because there is no way to grasp how, after “Israel dwelt,” and so forth, “and they took hold in it,” indicating their attachment to Egypt,

וְכָתוּב וַיִּפְרוּ וַיִּרְבּוּ שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה אָז עִיקַּר כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל וְכָתוּב וַיְחִי יַעֲקֹב שֶׁזֶּה הָיָה עִיקַּר הַחַיִּים שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב שֶׁנִּבְנָה כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל וְשִׁשִּׁים רִבּוֹא נְפָשׁוֹת שֶׁקִּבְּלוּ אַחַר כָּךְ הַתּוֹרָה וּבָזֶה אֵין שׁוּם תְּפִיסָה.

— it says, “They were fruitful and multiplied,” when the essential Congregation of Israel came into being; and “Jacob lived,” signifying his principal life, through the building of Israel’s congregation and the six hundred thousand souls that later received the Torah. This admits of no rational grasp.
וְעַל כֵּן לָא אִתְחֲזֵי לְאַפְרָשָׁא שֶׁאֵין כָּאן שׁוּם הֶפְסֵק פָּרָשָׁה כֵּיוָן שֶׁאֵין מָקוֹם לְהִתְבּוֹנֵן בָּזֶה.
— Therefore no separation should appear: there is no section break, since this is beyond reflective comprehension.
וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ זֶה יֵשׁ לְפָרֵשׁ כָּל טַעֲמֵי הַמִּדְרָשׁ רַבָּה.
— All the explanations in Midrash Rabbah can be understood along these lines.

p: דְּלִפְשׁוּטוֹ קָשֶׁה עַל טַעַם רִאשׁוֹן שֶׁהַפָּרָשָׁה סְתוּמָה מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהִתְחִיל הַשִּׁעְבּוּד וְהָא כָּל זְמַן שֶׁהָיָה אֶחָד מֵהַשְּׁבָטִים קַיָּים לֹא הִתְחִיל הַשִּׁעְבּוּד וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּפֵירוּשׁ רַבִּי שְׁלֹמֹה יִצְחָקִי וָאֵרָא דִּלְכָךְ נִמְנוּ שְׁנוֹתָיו שֶׁל לֵוִי וְכוּלֵי עַיֵּן שָׁם.

— On the plain level, the first explanation is difficult: the portion is closed because subjugation began, yet subjugation did not begin while any of the tribal ancestors remained alive. As Rashi explains in Va’era, Levi’s years were therefore enumerated, and so forth; see there.
וּבְמִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה (שְׁמוֹת) עַל פָּסוּק וַיָּמָת יוֹסֵף אִיתָא שֶׁכָּל זְמַן שֶׁהָיָה אֶחָד מֵהֶן מֵאוֹתָן שֶׁיָּרְדוּ לְמִצְרַיִם קַיָּים לֹא שִׁעְבְּדוּ הַמִּצְרִים בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל.
— Midrash Rabbah, Exodus, on “Joseph died,” teaches that as long as any of those who descended to Egypt remained alive, the Egyptians did not enslave Israel.
וּבִפְרָט כָּל זְמַן שֶׁיּוֹסֵף קַיָּים וְהָיָה מוֹשֵׁל הָאָרֶץ לֹא יִתָּכֵן שֶׁיְּשַׁעְבֵּד מִי בְּאֶחָיו.
— Especially while Joseph lived and ruled the land, it is inconceivable that anyone would enslave his brothers.
וְיוֹסֵף חַי אַחַר מִיתַת יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נ״ד שָׁנָה וְאֵיךְ אֶפְשָׁר לוֹמַר דְּאַחַר פְּטִירַת יַעֲקֹב הִתְחִיל הַשִּׁעְבּוּד.
— Joseph lived fifty-four years after our patriarch Jacob’s death; how, then, can it be said that subjugation began after Jacob passed away?
גַּם פְּשָׁט הַכָּתוּב וַיָּמָת יוֹסֵף וְגוֹמֵר וַיָּקָם מֶלֶךְ חָדָשׁ וְגוֹמֵר אֲשֶׁר לֹא יָדַע אֶת יוֹסֵף מַשְׁמַע שֶׁכָּל זְמַן שֶׁזָּכְרוּ אֶת יוֹסֵף לֹא מָלֵא לִבָּם לְשַׁעְבֵּד בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל.

— The plain meaning of “Joseph died,” and so forth, followed by “A new king arose,” and so forth, “who did not know Joseph,” also implies that while Joseph was remembered, they did not dare enslave Israel.
אַךְ הָעִנְיָן כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ בְּפֵירוּשׁ מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בְּמִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה מַה גְּאוּלָּה בְּכָל יוֹם
— The explanation follows our interpretation of Midrash Rabbah’s “redemption is daily”:
שֶׁהַמְכוּוָּן עַל הַגְּאוּלָּה מִקִּטְרוּג וְשִׁעְבּוּד הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע שֶׁזֶּהוּ עִיקַּר הַגְּאוּלָּה (וְנִתְבָּאֵר מַאֲמָר ג)
— it means redemption from the evil inclination’s accusation and enslavement, which is the essential redemption (explained in discourse 3).
וְכֵן כָּאן אַף דִּכְתִיב וַיֵּאָחֲזוּ בָהּ שֶׁהָיָה לָהֶם אֲחִיזָה בְּמִצְרַיִם
— Here too, although “they took hold in it” signifies attachment to Egypt,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם כָּל זְמַן שֶׁיַּעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הָיָה קַיָּם הוֹפִיעַ מֵחַיּוּת יַעֲקֹב לְהַכְּלָל.
— while Jacob remained alive, the vitality of Jacob shone upon the collective.
וְלֹא הִרְגִּישׁוּ כְּלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵעִנְיַן קְלִיפַּת מִצְרַיִם.
— Israel as a whole felt nothing of Egypt’s impure husk.
וְאַף שֶׁהָיָה לָהֶם אֲחִיזָה מָה בְּמִצְרַיִם הָיָה בְּהֶעְלֵם מְאֹד.
— Although they had some attachment to Egypt, it was deeply concealed.
וְכֵיוָן שֶׁנִּפְטַר יַעֲקֹב הִתְחִיל הַשִּׁעְבּוּד שֶׁהִתְחִילוּ לְהַרְגִּישׁ מִשִּׁעְבּוּד הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע מִקְּלִיפַּת מִצְרַיִם וְהִתְחִיל הֶעָמָל בְּמִלְחֶמֶת הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע.
— When Jacob passed away, subjugation began: they began to feel the evil inclination’s enslavement arising from Egypt’s impurity, and the toil of battling that inclination began.

h: The Closing of Wisdom and Understanding

p: וְזֶה שֶׁכָּתַב רַבִּי שְׁלֹמֹה יִצְחָקִי שֶׁכֵּיוָן שֶׁנִּפְטַר יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ נִסְתְּמוּ עֵינֵיהֶם וְלִבָּם שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל מִצָּרַת הַשִּׁעְבּוּד.
— Thus Rashi writes that when our father Jacob passed away, Israel’s eyes and hearts were closed by the distress of subjugation.
וְכֵן הַלָּשׁוֹן בַּזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בְּשַׁעֲתָא דְּמִית יַעֲקֹב אִסְתִּימוּ עֵינֵיהוֹן דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל.
— The holy Zohar likewise says, “When Jacob died, the eyes of Israel were closed.”

עֵינֵיהֶם מְרַמֵּז עַל בְּחִינַת חָכְמָה מוֹחָא דְּהָעֵינַיִם שָׁרְשָׁם מֵהַמּוֹחַ וְכֵן נִקְרְאוּ הַסַּנְהֶדְרִין וְחַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל עֵינֵי הָעֵדָה (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בָּבָא בַּתְרָא ד.) וְלִבָּם הַיְינוּ בְּחִינַת בִּינָה לִבָּא.

— Their eyes allude to Chokhmah, the mind, because the eyes are rooted in the brain; similarly, the Sanhedrin and Israel’s sages are called “the eyes of the congregation” (Bava Batra 4a). Their hearts signify Binah, understanding in the heart.
וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַקְּלִיפָּה נִסְתְּמוּ מַעְיְנוֹת חָכְמָה וּבִינָה מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל וְנִכְנַס לַלֵּב וָמוֹחַ הַשִּׁעְבּוּד מִקְּלִיפַּת מִצְרַיִם.
— Through impurity, the wellsprings of wisdom and understanding were closed off from Israel, and enslavement to Egypt’s impure husk entered their hearts and minds.
אַךְ מִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא הִרְגִּישׁוּ בִּמְפוֹרָשׁ שֶׁנִּתְקַלְקְלוּ עַל יְדֵי קְלִיפַּת מִצְרַיִם.
— Nevertheless, they did not clearly perceive that Egypt’s impurity had corrupted them.

רַק נִכְנַס לַלֵּב וָמוֹחַ וְלֹא הָיָה בְּהֶעְלֵם כָּל כָּךְ כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה בְּחַיֵּי יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וְעַל כֵּן פָּרָשָׁה זוֹ סְתוּמָה שֶׁלֹּא נִיתַּן לְהִתְבּוֹנֵן אֵיךְ שֶׁנֶּאֶחֱזוּ בִּקְלִיפַּת מִצְרַיִם בְּעוֹמֶק בַּמּוֹחַ וּבַלֵּב.

— It entered their hearts and minds and was no longer as deeply concealed as during Jacob’s lifetime. Therefore this portion is closed: one cannot fathom how they became attached to Egypt’s impurity in the depths of mind and heart.

p: וְכֵן טַעַם הַשֵּׁנִי שֶׁבְּמִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה שֶׁפָּרָשָׁה זוֹ סְתוּמָה מִפְּנֵי שֶׁבִּיקֵּשׁ יַעֲקֹב לְגַלּוֹת הַקֵּץ וְנִסְתַּם מִמֶּנּוּ.
— Likewise, the Midrash’s second explanation says that the portion is closed because Jacob wished to reveal the end and it was concealed from him.
גַּם כֵּן לִפְשׁוּטוֹ קָשֶׁה דְּהָיָה צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת סְתוּמָה פָּרָשַׁת וַיִּקְרָא יַעֲקֹב וְשָׁם מַתְחִיל פָּרָשָׁה וְהִיא פְּתוּחָה וּמַה טַּעַם שֶׁיִּהְיֶה וַיְחִי יַעֲקֹב סְתוּמָה.
— This too is difficult on the plain level: the section beginning “Jacob called” should then be closed, yet a new open section begins there. Why should “Jacob lived” be closed?
אַךְ בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (רלד ב) הִקְשָׁה לָמָּה נִכְתַּב בַּתּוֹרָה עִנְיָן זֶה שֶׁבִּיקֵּשׁ יַעֲקֹב לְגַלּוֹת הַקֵּץ וְנִסְתַּם מִמֶּנּוּ וְלָמָּה נִכְתַּב וְאַגִּידָה אִם לֹא נִתְקַיֵּים.
— The holy Zohar (234b) asks why the Torah records that Jacob wished to reveal the end but it was concealed from him. Why write “I will tell,” if it was not fulfilled?

אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת גִּילָּה לָהֶם זֶה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אַחֲרִית הַיָּמִים וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁבַּסּוֹף יִהְיֶה הַכֹּל לְטוֹבָה וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא יד:) בְּרוּת פּוּרְעָנוּת דְּאִית לֵיהּ אַחֲרִית וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁמִּמֶּנָּה יָצָא דָוִד וְזַרְעוֹ וּמָשִׁיחַ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הָאַחֲרִית לְטוֹבָה.

— In truth, he revealed that there would be an “end of days,” meaning that everything would ultimately be for good. This resembles Bava Batra 14b’s description of Ruth as “calamity with a future”: from her emerged David, his descendants, and the Messiah, making the outcome good.

וְכֵן בְּגָלוּת בָּבֶל כְּתִיב לָתֵת לָכֶם אַחֲרִית וְתִקְוָה וְדָרְשׁוּ (תַּעֲנִית כט:) אֵלּוּ דְּקָלִים וְכוּלֵי וְאָמַרְנוּ שֶׁרוֹמֵז לְתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה שֶׁהוּא מִין הָאַחֲרוֹן מִשִּׁבְעָה מִינִים שֶׁהֵם כְּנֶגֶד שֶׁבַע הַמִּדּוֹת.

— Concerning the Babylonian exile it likewise says, “To give you a future and hope,” which the Sages expounded (Ta’anit 29b) as date palms, and so forth. We explained that this alludes to the Oral Torah: dates are the last of the seven species, which correspond to the seven attributes.
וּבְבָבֶל הָיָה עִיקַּר הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה (כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר מַאֲמָר א) וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ וְאַגִּידָה לָכֶם דְּאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ רָזָא דְחָכְמְתָא אִיהוּ.
— The Oral Torah’s principal expansion took place in Babylonia (as explained in discourse 1). Thus “I will tell you,” which the holy Zohar describes as a mystery of wisdom,

אֵת אֲשֶׁר יִקְרָא אֶתְכֶם בְּאַחֲרִית הַיָּמִים הַיְינוּ דְּשִׁעְבּוּד מִצְרַיִם וְהַגָּלוּת יִהְיֶה הֲכָנָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לָכֶם אַחֲרִית לְטוֹבָה שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה יִזְכּוּ לְהַהִתְגַּלּוּת בִּקְרִיעַת יַם סוּף וּלְמַתַּן תּוֹרָה וְזֶה גִּילָּה לָהֶם בֶּאֱמֶת.

— “what will befall you at the end of days” means that Egyptian subjugation and exile would prepare a good future for them: through these they would merit the revelation at the splitting of the Sea and at the giving of the Torah. This he truly revealed.

אַךְ מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב שֶׁנִּסְתַּם מִמֶּנּוּ הוּא הַגְּאוּלָּה פְּלָאִים בְּחִינַת פֶּלֶא עֶלְיוֹן שֶׁהוּא דְּלֵית נְהוֹרָא אֶלָּא הַהוּא דְּנָפִיק מִגּוֹ חֲשׁוֹכָא (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב קפד א)
— What was concealed from him was the wondrous redemption, the supernal wonder: “There is no light except that which emerges from darkness” (Zohar II 184a).
וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁיָּאִיר לָהֶם אֵיךְ מִמַּה דִּכְתִיב וַיֵּשֶׁב יִשְׂרָאֵל וְגוֹמֵר וַיֵּאָחֲזוּ בָהּ וְגוֹמֵר
— He could not illuminate for them how “Israel dwelt,” and so forth, “and they took hold in it,”
שֶׁעַל יְדֵי שֶׁנֶּאֶחֱזוּ בְּמִצְרַיִם יִהְיֶה שְׁלֵימוּת הַכְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל וּכְמוֹ שֶׁרוֹמֵז וַיְחִי יַעֲקֹב וּמִזֶּה בָּאוּ לִכְלַל הָאַחֲרִית טוֹבָה.
— would mean that attachment to Egypt itself would perfect the Congregation of Israel, as “Jacob lived” alludes, bringing them to a good outcome.

שֶׁזֶּה נֶעְלַם מֵהֶם עַד שֶׁרָאוּ אַחַר כָּךְ עַיִן בְּעַיִן שֶׁעַל יְדֵי גָּלוּת מִצְרַיִם זָכוּ לְהִתְגַּלּוּת עַתִּיקָא בִּקְרִיעַת יַם סוּף וְרָאֲתָה שִׁפְחָה עַל הַיָּם מַה שֶּׁלֹּא רָאָה יְחֶזְקֵאל (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּמְּכִילְתָּא בְּשַׁלַּח וְזֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ שָׁם סד ב) וְכֵן אַחַר כָּךְ זָכוּ לְהִתְגַּלּוּת מַתַּן תּוֹרָה.

— This remained hidden from them until they later saw directly that the Egyptian exile led to the revelation of Atika at the splitting of the Sea. A maidservant at the Sea saw what Ezekiel did not (as stated in Mekhilta, Beshalach, and the holy Zohar there, 64b). Afterward they likewise merited the revelation at the giving of the Torah.
וְעַל כֵּן בְּכָאן פָּרָשָׁה סְתוּמָה שֶׁלֹּא נִיתַּן לְהִתְבּוֹנֵן בָּזֶה אֵיךְ שֶׁנִּסְתָּעֵף הָאוֹר מִתּוֹךְ הַחוֹשֶׁךְ.
— Therefore the portion is closed here: one cannot comprehend how light branches forth from within darkness.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I, 234b: ““He said”—what is meant by “he said”? We have explained it, as in “You will say in your heart”: speech in a whisper. “Gather yourselves”: should it not say “Gather,” as in “Gather My faithful ones to Me”? Rather, we know that “Gather yourselves” comes from the place above: gather yourselves in a complete bond, in a single unity. “I will tell you”—what does “I will tell” mean? It is a mystery of wisdom. Rabbi Yosei asked Rabbi Shimon: We learned that “I will tell,” “he told,” “they will tell,” and similar forms are a mystery of wisdom. Why does this expression embody a mystery of wisdom? He answered: Because the letters gimel and dalet come together without separation. This is the mystery of wisdom: a word that comes in completeness through the mystery of the letters is such when they are in wisdom. But dalet without gimel is not complete, nor is gimel without dalet. They are bound to one another without separation; whoever separates them brings death upon himself, and this is the mystery of Adam’s sin. Therefore this expression is a mystery of wisdom. Although a yod sometimes stands between gimel and dalet, it causes no separation: everything is a single bond. Thus the expression is certainly precise. “I will tell you”—a mystery of wisdom: he wished to reveal the final outcome of all Israel’s deeds.”

וְהוּא דְּאַף שֶׁהָיָה נֶעְלָם מֵהַכְּלָל אֵיךְ יִהְיֶה מִמַּה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר וַיֵּשֶׁב יִשְׂרָאֵל וְגוֹמֵר וַיֵּאָחֲזוּ בָהּ אַחֲרִית הַיָּמִים.
— Although the collective could not see how “Israel dwelt,” and so forth, “and they took hold in it,” would bring about the end of days,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם יַעֲקֹב בְּעַצְמוֹ יָדַע שֶׁמִּגָּלוּת מִצְרַיִם יִהְיֶה עִיקַּר הַיְשׁוּעָה וּצְמִיחַת כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל וְסָתַם מִמֶּנּוּ כָּל צָרוֹת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם.
— Jacob himself knew that Egypt’s exile would bring the principal salvation and the growth of Israel’s congregation. Thus all the world’s troubles were closed off from him.

— He knew that everything was for good. Yet there is no section break for reflection, because the ability to show this and illuminate it within every individual Israelite’s heart was withheld from him: each could not recognize, in the present, the goodness concealed within it.

— Shabbat resembles the World to Come and contains a revelation of Atika. “On the day Hashem grants you rest,” and so forth, “and from the hard labor,” and so forth, is interpreted by the holy Zohar (I 48b, beginning) as the day of Shabbat, the day of granting rest.
וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁאַף שֶׁהוּא עֲדַיִין בְּהָעֲבוֹדָה הַקָּשָׁה וְעִיקַּר הָעִנְיָן נֶעְלָם וְלֹא נִיתַּן לְהִתְבּוֹנֵן בּוֹ אֵיךְ הוּא לְטוֹבָה.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I, 48a–b: “Rabbi Shimon said further: Concerning this we learned that Shabbat resembles the World to Come. It is indeed so. Just as the sabbatical year and the Jubilee resemble one another, so do Shabbat and the World to Come. That addition to the soul comes from the mystery of “Remember” to this shelter of peace, which receives from the World to Come; it gives this addition to the holy world. Through that addition they rejoice, and all weekday affairs, all sorrow, and all distress are forgotten, as it says: “On the day that Hashem gives you rest from your sorrow, your agitation, and the hard service.””

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Tiferet Yosef, Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot §1: “Although in this world Shabbat seems to a person a great restriction—for during the week a person prepares all the necessities of food, bread to eat and clothing to wear, while on Shabbat all this is forbidden, so that in this world it seems a great restriction—in its depth Shabbat alludes to the day that is entirely Shabbat and rest for eternal life. Shabbat alludes to what the Talmud says: ‘In the future, the Land of Israel will produce ready-made loaves and fine woolen garments.’ This means that a person will not need the instruments of his labor. For of Shabbat the holy Zohar says, ‘From it the higher days are blessed.’ At the root, a person then receives the power of service for all six weekdays.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Shabbat’s present restriction carries the form of a future freedom from the need to labor. This clarifies how the heart can already taste rest and goodness on Shabbat while the way concealment will become revelation remains beyond present understanding.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah 15:2: “It follows what is said in the Gemara (Pesachim 50a): ‘On that day Hashem will be One’—is He then not One today? … In the World to Come it will be entirely ‘Who is good and does good.’ That is, ‘Havayah is One’ shows that everything is for good, for this Name denotes mercy and the wish only to do good; only in this world it is not revealed so that people recognize the good in its opposite as well, and this will be revealed only ‘on that day.’ In the days of the Hasmoneans they had rest in the aspect of the higher unification, for they all recognized that the decree had been for their good, since through it they defeated the Greeks and threw off their yoke. … So too of Shabbat it is written, ‘On the day Hashem grants you rest from your sorrow and from your trouble and from the hard labor,’ which is expounded (Zohar I 48b and elsewhere) as the Shabbat day, the day of granting rest. That is, it holds a revelation of the light created on the first day, of which it is written, ‘God saw the light, that it was good’; then one merits to grasp that everything is for good, and even while he is within the hard labor he has rest, since it is for good.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Chanukah 15 reads the same verse and Zohar so that Shabbat’s rest is the grasp that everything is for good even in the midst of the hard labor. It adds the Hasmoneans, who came to see that the decree itself had been for their good, and ties this to Pesachim 50a’s “Who is good and does good.”
